meta.case_name: New England Grocery Chain – Home Delivery

prompt.context: A grocery chain in New England is considering offering an Internet delivery service (i.e., groceries can be ordered via the Internet and delivered directly to your home). Including the client, there are three main grocery chains in the area. One of them has already entered the Internet market. The only other grocery store currently offering Internet delivery service in the U.S. is a Midwest store.
prompt.question: Should the client enter this market? If so, what issues would they face? If not, how should they protect their market share?

clarifying_info.q: When did the regional competitor begin their Internet delivery service and how successful have they been?
clarifying_info.a: They began about 6 months ago and approximately 1% of their sales are from the Internet. However, they are forecasting that number to grow.

clarifying_info.q: Have our stores experienced any reduction in traffic over the last 6 months?
clarifying_info.a: Well, perhaps a very small drop, but it's hard to say.

clarifying_info.q: Are the competitor's Internet prices the same or higher than their retail store prices?
clarifying_info.a: Prices have been mixed with no noticeable trend. They are still trying to determine if they can justify a premium.

framework: Competitor analysis: assess the regional competitor's strategy, pricing, and early market traction
Consumer demand: survey current customers and potential new customers to gauge interest, willingness to pay a premium, and risk of cannibalization
Cost analysis: identify and evaluate all costs of running the service (technology, delivery, personnel, insurance, inventory/warehousing)
Go/no-go recommendation: synthesize findings to decide whether to enter, and if not, how to protect market share

questions.prompt: What do we know about the regional competitor's Internet delivery performance, and what does it tell us?
questions.guidance: The competitor launched 6 months ago; only 1% of sales come from Internet — very small. Could indicate early-stage trend or low consumer interest. Pricing strategy is unsettled (no premium established). Client stores have seen at most a very small traffic drop. Conclusion: insufficient signal to be certain the service is commercially viable, but the competitor is still in early stages.

questions.prompt: How would you assess consumer demand and estimate potential market size?
questions.guidance: Conduct surveys of current customers to measure interest and willingness to pay a premium. Identify non-customers: cross-reference area residents with credit cards, loyalty cards, checks received to find people not currently shopping at client stores. Survey potential new customers to assess incremental demand. Use survey results to estimate market size accounting for cannibalization and pricing effects.

questions.prompt: What costs would the client incur if it launches the Internet delivery service?
questions.guidance: Key cost categories: (1) technology — server setup and ongoing maintenance; (2) delivery personnel and order-processing staff; (3) insurance for delivery staff; (4) inventory warehousing. The largest concern is inventory: client must stock retail shelves AND maintain inventory for the delivery service. Three warehousing options to evaluate: (a) use retail stores — disfavored because it reduces retail selling space and stores likely lack capacity; (b) use existing warehouse distribution centers — preferred for initial launch, provided they are strategically located and have spare capacity; (c) build a dedicated warehouse — costly (construction, staffing, training) and only justified if demand proves sustainable and sizable.

questions.prompt: What is your final recommendation, and how should the client protect market share if it chooses not to enter?
questions.guidance: Recommendation to enter (conditional): if surveys show at least some demand and existing distribution centers have spare capacity, the client should pilot the service. Incremental cost is low using existing infrastructure, and early participation positions the client if the trend grows. If demand is low or the client opts out: protect market share by emphasizing the in-store experience — advertising the pleasure of in-store shopping vs. ordering from a screen; using survey insights to improve store attributes (music, cleanliness, staff friendliness) to retain customers and make the retail experience more attractive than the online alternative.

brainstorming.prompt: What costs and operational issues would the client face in running an Internet delivery service?

categories.name: Delivery & Logistics
ideas: Delivery vehicle fleet or third-party delivery contracts

categories.name: Inventory & Warehousing
ideas: Dedicated inventory separate from retail stock
Storage location decision (retail stores vs. existing distribution centers vs. new warehouse)

categories.name: Staffing
ideas: Customer service staff for online orders

categories.name: Marketing & Pricing
ideas: Customer acquisition for new online channel
Pricing strategy (same as in-store, premium, or discount)

recommendation: If surveys reveal meaningful consumer demand and existing distribution centers have available capacity, pilot the Internet delivery service using current infrastructure to minimize upfront cost and test viability
If demand appears low or infrastructure is insufficient, do not enter the market at this time
risks: Low consumer adoption makes the service unprofitable
Cannibalization of in-store sales without offsetting new revenue
Competitor scales quickly, making it harder for the client to catch up later
Inventory management complexity increases operational costs beyond projections
next_steps: Conduct consumer surveys of current and potential customers to quantify demand and willingness to pay a premium
Audit existing distribution center capacity and locations relative to target delivery areas
Model unit economics of the delivery service under conservative, base, and optimistic demand scenarios
If not entering: design a retail experience improvement program based on survey insights to protect existing market share
